# OMB M-25-21 — Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust

> **Federal policy, not NASA governance: binding on agencies as federal policy, a separate
> question from what NASA's own directives require.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary.
> It never by itself establishes what a specific NASA directive requires, and must not be
> cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | Office of Management and Budget (OMB), Executive Office of the President; signed by OMB Director Russell T. Vought |
| **Kind** | Policy memo (OMB Memorandum) |
| **Status** | Dated and effective April 3, 2025 [p.1]. Verified in the document text: "This memorandum rescinds and replaces Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Memorandum M-24-10, Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence" [p.1, Overview]. It implements Executive Order 14179. Currently in force. |
| **Where to get it** | whitehouse.gov (OMB memoranda), free public. Public copy, confirmed anonymously off-network on 2026-10-26: `https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf` |
| **Binds whom** | Verbatim: "This memorandum is directed to the heads of all Executive Branch departments and agencies, including independent regulatory agencies" [p.1, Scope] |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** (our reading) Of the five documents in this set, this is the one closest in shape to an assurance regime: it defines a risk-tiered category ("high-impact AI") with concrete required practices — impact assessment, independent review, ongoing monitoring, waiver tracking — comparable in structure, though not in content, to NASA mission-assurance gating. It is useful for seeing what the federal government requires of agency AI use generally; it says nothing about what any specific NASA directive requires.

**Key content for artificial intelligence / machine-learning assurance.**
- [p.10] Sec. 3(a)(i): "Chief AI Officers. Within 60 days of the issuance of this memorandum, the head of each agency must retain or designate a Chief AI Officer (CAIO). CAIOs will promote AI innovation, adoption, and governance, in coordination with appropriate agency officials."
- [p.13] Sec. 3(c): "Chief AI Officer Council. Within 90 days of the issuance of this memorandum, the Director of OMB, or designated senior official within OMB, shall convene and chair an interagency council to coordinate the development and use of AI in agencies' programs and operations..."
- [p.3] Overview: "agencies are directed to implement minimum risk management practices for AI that could have significant impacts when deployed (\"high-impact AI\"), as outlined in the Appendix... When the high-impact AI is not performing at an appropriate level, agencies must have a plan to discontinue its use."
- [p.14] Sec. 4(a): "A high-impact determination is possible whether there is or is not human oversight for the decision or action," and Sec. 6 lists use-case categories "automatically presumed to be high-impact" (e.g., safety-critical infrastructure control, biometric identification, benefits adjudication) [p.21-22].
- [p.14] Sec. 4(b): "Agencies are required to implement minimum risk management practices, detailed in Section 4(b) of this memorandum, to manage risks from high-impact AI use cases."
- [p.16] Sec. 4(a): "Authorizing Waivers from Minimum Practices for High-Impact AI. In coordination with other relevant officials, an agency CAIO may waive one or more of the requirements in this section... An agency CAIO... must certify the ongoing validity of each waiver on an annual basis."
- AI touchpoints found by keyword grep: pervasive throughout, as expected for a document whose whole subject is agency AI use — "AI" and "artificial intelligence" appear in nearly every section; "automat..." appears in the context of automated decision pipelines; "algorithm" and "machine learning" are not used as defined terms (the memo works from its own "AI" definition rather than those narrower terms).

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** No direct counterpart on the current NASA document list; federal agency policy and NASA's own internal directives are kept as separate coverage axes in this project (our reading) — the nearest topical neighbor would be NPR 7150.2D (NASA's software engineering requirements), since both set mandatory practices tied to risk/criticality tiers, but it answers a different question (what NASA requires of its own software vs. what federal policy requires of agency AI use generally).
